Subsurface Ocean. A body of liquid water hidden beneath the solid icy crust of a moon or planetary body. These oceans, potentially harboring life, exist in the outer solar system on Europa, Jupiter's moon; Enceladus, Saturn's moon; Ganymede, also orbiting Jupiter; and others. Kept liquid by internal tidal heating and radioactive decay rather than surface warmth, subsurface oceans represent one of the most compelling targets in the search for extraterrestrial microbial life.

Europa's subsurface ocean may contain twice as much liquid water as all of Earth's oceans combined. Tidal forces from the host planet's gravity continuously flex the moon, generating internal heat that prevents freezing.

Enceladus shoots geysers of water vapor directly from its subsurface ocean through cracks in its crust, making it observable from orbit. Ganymede, the largest moon in the solar system, is believed to host a multilayered ocean system sandwiched between ice shells.

The interface between subsurface water and rocky seafloors may support chemosynthetic ecosystems independent of sunlight. NASA and ESA missions including Europa Clipper and JUICE are designed to detect chemical signs of habitability and life.

Unlike Earth's oceans, subsurface moons lack direct sunlight but exploit chemical gradients and hydrothermal vents for energy. Ocean circulation on these moons may be driven by convection and tidal pumping rather than wind-driven currents. The depth and salinity of subsurface oceans can be inferred from magnetic field measurements, revealing internal structure without drilling.
